subject: Vocabulary
topic: Word Pairs — Confused and Misused Words

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'The committee will ______ the proposal tomorrow.'

options.option_text: access (wrong: access = to gain entry to; you don't 'access' a proposal)
assess (correct: assess = to evaluate or judge; 'assess the proposal' = evaluate it ✓)
excess (wrong: excess = an amount more than necessary; not a verb here)
egress (wrong: egress = an exit or means of going out)

questions.explanation: B is correct. ASSESS = to evaluate, judge, or calculate. 'Assess the proposal' = evaluate its merits. ACCESS = enter or obtain. Don't confuse: access (noun/verb = entry), assess (verb = evaluate), excess (noun/adjective = too much), egress (noun = exit).

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'The journalist tried to ______ information from the reluctant witness.'

options.option_text: illicit (wrong: illicit = illegal, unlawful — adjective, not a verb)
elicit (correct: elicit = to draw out or evoke a response; 'elicit information' ✓)
solicit (wrong: solicit = to request/ask formally; though possible, 'elicit' is the precise word for 'drawing out')
explicit (wrong: explicit = clear and detailed; adjective — not a verb)

questions.explanation: B is correct. ELICIT (verb) = to draw out or evoke a response, information, or reaction. 'Elicit information' = draw it out. ILLICIT (adjective) = forbidden by law or rules. Very commonly confused pair: ELICIT (draw out) vs ILLICIT (illegal). Memory: eLICIT = draw out LICensed info; iLLICIT = iLLegal.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'The CEO ______ all employees to submit their reports by Friday.'

options.option_text: implied (wrong: implied = suggested indirectly; the CEO didn't indirectly suggest it)
inferred (wrong: inferred = concluded from evidence; you infer as a LISTENER, not speaker)
requested (wrong: too weak — the CEO may have used stronger language)
directed (correct: directed = officially ordered/instructed; 'directed all employees to submit' ✓)

questions.explanation: D is correct. DIRECTED = officially ordered or instructed. Key distinction: IMPLY (speaker hints/suggests) vs INFER (listener concludes). 'He implied' = he suggested. 'She inferred' = she concluded. A CEO would DIRECT employees, not imply or infer.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'She felt a strong ______ to quit her job and travel the world.'

options.option_text: impulse (correct: impulse = a sudden strong desire or urge to do something ✓)
compulsive (wrong: compulsive = adjective describing an irresistible urge; wrong part of speech here)
impulsive (wrong: impulsive = adjective; can't fill this noun position)
compulsion (compulsion = a very strong force that makes you do something; could work but 'impulse' is more natural for a sudden feeling)

questions.explanation: A is correct. IMPULSE (noun) = a sudden strong desire or urge. 'An impulse to quit' = a sudden urge. IMPULSIVE (adjective) = acting on impulse. COMPULSION (noun) = a strong irresistible urge (stronger than impulse, often repeated). 'She felt a strong impulse' is the most natural phrasing for a sudden desire.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'The police officer ______ the suspect for two hours before releasing him.'

options.option_text: interrogated (correct: interrogate = to question formally and officially, often under pressure ✓)
interview (wrong: interview = a formal meeting to discuss something; less confrontational)
conversed (wrong: conversed = had a conversation; too informal)
discussed (wrong: discussed = talked about; too neutral for police questioning of a suspect)

questions.explanation: A is correct. INTERROGATE = to question someone intensely, especially a suspect or witness in a police or military context. 'Interrogated the suspect' = questioned formally and persistently. Distinguish: interview (friendly/professional), interrogate (forceful/investigative), cross-examine (in court), question (neutral).

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'His constant interruptions ______ our ability to complete the task.',

options.option_text: inhibited (correct: inhibit = to restrict or prevent something from happening ✓)
prohibited (wrong: prohibit = to formally forbid; interruptions don't formally forbid things)
facilitated (wrong: facilitate = to make easier; interruptions don't facilitate tasks)
exhibited (wrong: exhibit = to display; doesn't fit the context)

questions.explanation: A is correct. INHIBIT = to restrict, hinder, or prevent something. 'Inhibited our ability' = prevented or restricted our ability. PROHIBIT = to officially forbid (requires legal authority). FACILITATE = to make easier (opposite of inhibit). Inhibit ↔ Facilitate are antonyms.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'The prime minister's speech was designed to ______ the voters.'

options.option_text: persuade (correct: persuade = to convince someone to believe or do something through argument ✓)
peruse (wrong: peruse = to read carefully; unrelated to a speech's effect on voters)
pursue (wrong: pursue = to follow or chase; doesn't fit)
pervade (wrong: pervade = to spread through; not about convincing voters)

questions.explanation: A is correct. PERSUADE = to convince someone through argument or reasoning. 'Designed to persuade voters' = intended to convince them. Confused words: persuade (convince), peruse (read carefully — NOT skim), pursue (chase), pervade (spread throughout). PERUSE is particularly trap-worthy: it means thorough reading, not casual reading.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'The new policy will ______ the old one from next month.'

options.option_text: supersede (correct: supersede = to take the place of; replace ✓)
supercede (wrong: 'supercede' is a common misspelling; correct spelling is 'supersede')
precede (wrong: precede = to come before; opposite of replacing)
proceed (wrong: proceed = to continue forward; unrelated to replacement)

questions.explanation: A is correct. SUPERSEDE = to take the place of; to replace (especially something outdated). Note the spelling: supersEDE (not 'supercede'). From Latin: super (above) + sede (seat) = to sit above/replace. 'The new policy supersedes the old one.' The 'supercede' spelling is one of the most common misspellings in English.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'The discovery of oil has ______ the economy of the region.'

options.option_text: transformed (correct: transform = to change dramatically in form or character ✓)
conformed (wrong: conform = to obey rules or meet standards; doesn't fit the discovery context)
informed (wrong: inform = to tell; the oil didn't tell the economy something)
performed (wrong: perform = to carry out; doesn't fit)

questions.explanation: A is correct. TRANSFORM = to make a dramatic change in the form, appearance, or character of something. 'Discovery of oil transformed the economy' = changed it dramatically. The -form verb family: transform (change dramatically), reform (improve/change), conform (comply with norms), inform (tell), perform (do/execute).

questions.stem: Choose the correctly used word: 'The politician's remarks were ______, angering many in the crowd.'

options.option_text: inflammatory (correct: inflammatory = arousing anger or controversy; 'inflammatory remarks' that anger people ✓)
flammable (wrong: flammable = easily set on fire; literal meaning, not figurative)
flameless (wrong: flameless = without a flame; wrong context)
inflammable (wrong: inflammable also means easily set on fire; same as flammable — not figurative)

questions.explanation: A is correct. INFLAMMATORY = arousing or intended to arouse strong feelings of anger or passion; provocative. 'Inflammatory remarks' = statements that inflame (provoke) people's anger. FLAMMABLE and INFLAMMABLE both mean 'easily set on fire' (physical property). Note: in English, INFLAMMABLE does NOT mean 'not flammable' — it IS flammable.
